newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: People must come first in information society - EU.
newsitem.headline: People must come first in information society - EU.

text.p: The European Union must avoid letting a gap open up in the emerging information society and ensure that people come first, EU social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn said on Monday.

Flynn, in Dublin to launch an EU green paper called "Living and Working in the European Information Society - People First", said the information society should enrich life, not erode its essential humanity.
"Quality of life ultimately depends on relations between people, families and communities, not the efficiency with which we use machines or material wealth," he said.

The green paper sets out the debate on information technology and invites comments from interested parties before the EU Commission brings forward an action plan for the development of the European information society.
Flynn said that many people were concerned about the possible impact of new technology on their lives and viewed it as threat to their future.

"We want to make people part of this process of change, give them an opportunity of contributing and also identify ways of countering the risks so that we can make best use of all the opportunities that come from the information society," he told a news conference.
The green paper focuses on the three areas of work, employment and living in the information society.
Flynn said that, while new technology will destroy some jobs, it will also create new jobs although people will have to be provided with new skills.

"The challenge of radically overhauling our education and training systems has to be taken on board. We do not want a two-speed labour market between those who have access and those who don't have the skills and the knowledge," he said.
The launch of the green paper coincided with the start of a two-day colloquium on the information society attended by around 300 participants from EU member states.

The colloquium, which can receive input via the internet from people unable to attend in person, was designed to shift the focus from what technology can do to how it can meet the needs and wants of Europe's citizens.
